title: Constexpr variables
recap: A constexpr variable is a compile-time constant and must be initialized with a constant expression. It is implicitly const, so writing both constexpr and const on an ordinary variable is redundant.

Use constexpr for constant variables whose values are known at compile time. Use const for runtime constants whose initializers are not constant expressions; detailed constexpr function rules are covered later in Chapter F.
objectives: Declare non-integral and integral compile-time constants with constexpr.
Build one constexpr variable from other constexpr variables.
Keep a value derived from a mutable runtime variable const rather than constexpr.
Validate a constexpr calculation with static_assert without defining constexpr functions.
warnings: A const double is not usable in a constant expression merely because it has a literal initializer.
A value initialized from a mutable variable is a runtime value and should not be declared constexpr.
Do not introduce a constexpr function; this exercise is about variable declarations.
challenge: Declare unitCost, packageCount, and totalCost as constexpr variables so their product can be checked by static_assert. Keep currentVisitors mutable and snapshotVisitors const because that snapshot is initialized from a runtime variable. Preserve the deterministic report and do not introduce constexpr functions.
hints: The static_assert fails because const floating-point variables are not automatically usable in constant expressions.
Replace const with constexpr on unitCost, packageCount, and totalCost; totalCost should remain their product.
Do not make snapshotVisitors constexpr: its initializer currentVisitors is mutable, so const correctly expresses a runtime snapshot that cannot later change.
